questions.question: Explain what a telescope does and describe it as a system.
questions.expected_answer: A telescope collects much more light than our eyes can, because its lens or mirror is much wider than our pupil, so faint objects become visible. It also magnifies, making distant objects look bigger and clearer. As a system, its input is light from space, its process is collecting and focusing the light with lenses or mirrors, and its output is a clear image seen by an eye or recorded by a camera.

questions.question: What is the difference between a refracting telescope and a reflecting telescope?
questions.expected_answer: A refracting telescope uses lenses, curved pieces of clear glass that bend light: a big lens collects the light and an eyepiece magnifies the image. Galileo used a refractor. A reflecting telescope uses a curved mirror to collect light and reflect it to a point, where an eyepiece or camera picks it up. Most big modern telescopes are reflectors, because big mirrors can be supported from behind.

questions.question: Why are some telescopes built on high mountains or sent into space, and what kinds of information do telescopes gather?
questions.expected_answer: The air blurs starlight, and clouds, dust and city lights get in the way, so telescopes work best high up in dry places far from cities, or in space above the air, like the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes. Telescopes show us what objects in space look like, help scientists find out what stars are made of, how hot and how far away they are, find planets around other stars, and watch for asteroids.
